new_statements.quote: p. 36: "In an ordinary word, the ultima is the nucleus. The ultima carries tone and has a much greater potential for consonant, vowel, and prosodic contrasts that[n] does a nonultima." p. 49 (1.4): "One of these is the phonological PHRASE, a level marked by a stress on the ultima of the word which functions as its nucleus. [...] Whatever the number of words in a phrase, stress occurs on either the first or second word. Phrase stress /'/ is marked both by intensity on the ultima of the word receiving it and by a lengthening of unchecked long vowels or a shortening of short vowels." p. 50 (2, SAC): "Words have stress on the ultima. There is also a phonetic stress on a penult with tone 2, and on a penult preceding an ultima with a medially-checked vowel (V?V or VhV)."

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement (final syllable) as the catalog, but the explicit stress statement for Copala is framed at the phrase level (stress on the ultima of the phrase nucleus) rather than as a word-stress rule; it adds prominence of tone-3 nonultimas and the exclamatory-word pitch-stress patterns. The sentence 'Words have stress on the ultima' is about Chicahuaxtla Trique, not Copala.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Copala (SJC) the ultima is the nucleus of the word and carries all the tonal, consonantal, vocalic and prosodic contrasts; the stress that Hollenbach explicitly locates is the phonological-phrase stress, which falls on the ultima of the phrase's nucleus word (intensity plus vowel lengthening/shortening), with a stronger utterance stress on one phrase. For the other dialect (SAC Chicahuaxtla) she says outright that words are stressed on the ultima.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 45: 'Tone-carrying nonultimas with /3/ are more prominent than non-tone-carrying nonultimas.' For SAC a phonetic penult stress with tone 2 or before a medially-checked ultima; for SJC exclamatory (utterance-final) words replace the eight-contour tone system by five 'pitch-stress patterns', one of which has level tone on the penult (p. 47-48).
new_statements.exceptions: Exclamatory (utterance-final) words have a different prosodic structure (sec. 1.3); a few words have a contrastive tone on a nonultima (fused compounds, Spanish loans), p. 36.
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe San Juan Copala Trique (Hollenbach 1992, p. 179: no discernible geographic variation within Copala Trique, though much idiolectal variation). Hollenbach 1977 also describes San Andrés Chicahuaxtla Trique (SAC), a different Trique language; its sentence 'Words have stress on the ultima. There is also a phonetic stress on a penult with tone 2..' (p. 50) is about Chicahuaxtla, not Copala. The Bradley & Hollenbach 1992 volume also contains a Yosondúa Mixtec sketch (Farris), not about this language.

new_statements.quote: p. 15: "En todas las palabras del triqui de Copala la última sílaba se pronuncia con mayor fuerza, tanto las que terminan con una vocal como las que terminan con una consonante, cualquiera que sea el patrón tonal. Así que, no es necesario escribir el acento. Las palabras que tienen el tono 3 o el tono 5 en una sílaba no final tienen un acento secundario en esta sílaba. Este acento tampoco se escribe." p. 32: "Cuando otros sustantivos se usan como vocativos, cambian el acento prosódico de la sílaba final a una sílaba anterior; y muchas veces su tono cambia."
new_statements.translation: p. 15: "In all words of Copala Triqui the last syllable is pronounced with greater force, both those that end in a vowel and those that end in a consonant, whatever the tone pattern. So it is not necessary to write the accent. Words that have tone 3 or tone 5 on a non-final syllable have a secondary stress on that syllable. This accent is not written either." p. 32: "When other nouns are used as vocatives, they shift the prosodic stress from the final syllable to an earlier syllable, and often their tone changes."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is always on the last syllable regardless of syllable shape or tone pattern; a secondary stress falls on any non-final syllable that carries contrastive tone 3 or 5; vocative forms of nouns move the stress to an earlier syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on non-final syllables bearing tone 3 or tone 5 (p. 14-15).
new_statements.exceptions: Vocative nouns shift stress from the final to an earlier syllable (p. 32, example chu³vee³² '¡perro!' vs chuvee³ 'perro'); Spanish loans keep only tonal/length reflexes of the Spanish accent, not a stress shift (sec. 2.7, p. 16).

readall_conflicts: No source disagrees on placement. Hollenbach's 2008 Gramática popular (sec. 2.6, p. 15) states word-level final stress for every word with secondary stress on non-final tone-3/tone-5 syllables and a vocative exception; Hollenbach 1977 locates Copala stress explicitly at the phrase level (stress on the ultima of the phrase-nucleus word, p. 49) and only says 'Words have stress on the ultima' for the Chicahuaxtla dialect (p. 50), so the 1977 paper is compatible but weaker as a word-stress statement. Rodriguez 2021 and Hollenbach 1992 are silent on stress and describe a tone language whose contrasts are confined to the final syllable; DiCanio 2008 (already held by the project from the earlier reading, not in this works list) reads Hollenbach 1977/1984b as 'final syllable prominence' for Copala. The only wrinkle is the vocative stress shift and the penult-contrastive lexical exceptions (chana 'woman', snó'o 'man'), which Hollenbach 2008 treats as exceptions rather than a different rule.
